newsitem.title: CHINA: China regrets rights censure move in U.N..
newsitem.headline: China regrets rights censure move in U.N..

text.p: China voiced regret on Friday at a move by the United States and Denmark to table a joint resolution criticising China's human rights record in the United Nations and warned relations could suffer.
Ties with Denmark would be damaged, Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said when asked about China's response to the tabling of the motion on Thursday in Geneva.
"They have deliberately resorted to confrontation by co-sponsoring the motion and we feel great regret at their move," he said.

"We are not afraid of confrontations, but as a result the confrontations only will harm relations between China and those countries that take the lead in sponsoring the anti-China motions," Shen warned.

Beijing stopped short of saying the move to push for a motion that calls on China to release political prisoners and to protect the cultural and ethnic identity of Tibetans and others would harm slowly warming ties with the United States.

China's response to the U.S. decision to support Denmark in tabling the resolution to censure China in the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva this month was unusually restrained, reflecting improved relations, diplomats said.

The United States and China have moved painstakingly in recent months to ease strains over disputes ranging from Taiwan to trade and human rights that chilled their relationship in 1995 and early 1996.

U.S. Vice-President Al Gore visited China last month and reassured Beijing that the administration remained committed to an exchange of visits by President Clinton and China's President Jiang Zemin over the next two years.
Beijing appeared eager to try to limit damage to slowly improving U.S. relations, but lashed out instead at Denmark, which was the driving force behind the motion.
"We believe the decision taken by Denmark will cause damage to the bilateral relations between China and Denmark," Shen said.

Countries, such as Denmark, the Netherlands and the United States that co-sponsored the resolution "ignored the tremendous progress that the Chinese government has made in protecting the Chinese people's human rights in the last few decades", he said.
These countries had "neglected the sincerity of the Chinese government to resolve existing disputes through dialogue".

"The position of the Chinese government is quite clear," he Shen said. "China has made huge progress in protecting the Chinese people's basic rights and fundamental freedoms and in the future the Chinese government will make even greater efforts.
"However, Denmark has ignored all these efforts and opted for a confrontational approach," he said. "This we believe will inevitably cause harm to the bilateral relationship."

However, in Geneva, diplomatic sources said support for the Western-backed motion seemed to be eroding, making it increasingly likely that Beijing will escape censure again for the seventh straight year when the 53-member forum votes next Tuesday.

Australia announced it had struck a deal with China to set up a formal bilateral dialogue on human rights, and revealed it would no longer back the Danish motion. Canada has also edged away from co-sponsoring the text, diplomats said.
No developing country co-sponsored the Danish text -- an indication they are lining up behind Beijing, diplomats said.
A total of 15 states co-sponsored the resolution, including 10 European Union member states, but the United States and Denmark were hoping for more co-sponsors by Tuesday's vote.
